excerpt: Hyrax AI learns a whole codebase, audits it across security, correctness, maintainability, performance, architecture and operations, and returns fixes as pull requests that an engineer reviews and merges. What it does, what we could and couldn't confirm, and alternatives.
content:
Hyrax AI describes itself as a codebase architect for engineering teams. It connects to a repository, learns the whole codebase, applies architectural judgment to changes and returns each fix as a pull request. Its Product Hunt listing stresses that nothing auto-merges: an engineer reviews and merges every one.

Hyrax's launch images add detail. A full audit runs about 39 tools across six categories (security, correctness, maintainability, performance, architecture and operations), and findings are scored by severity and effort so easy wins come first. Each finding has to survive an internal pass that argues against it and cite the exact lines involved. For a fix, Hyrax runs the repository's own tests and build, reviews its own diff, opens the pull request as a draft and marks it ready once CI passes. Its GitHub organisation describes it as automated code review and remediation.

This was Hyrax AI's second Product Hunt launch. It went live on 21 September 2026 and finished #5 for the day with 216 upvotes and 15 comments. Hyrax's home page returned an access error to us, but its documentation site (docs.hyrax.dev) is public. It describes Hyrax as a hosted service with no self-hosted option, says every connected repository gets automatic pull-request review, and lists a free plan and a paid plan at $30 per seat a month. According to its compliance page, Hyrax is built and operated by Iru and is in scope of Iru's SOC 2 Type II programme, with the first Type II report due after the observation window that runs to June 2027.

We have not tested Hyrax AI ourselves. This page brings together its Product Hunt page and launch images, its documentation site, its GitHub organisation and the official pages of comparable tools, and says where each fact comes from.

profile.platform: Connects to your code repository (GitHub organisation listed)
profile.summary_short: AI that audits a whole codebase and returns verified fixes as pull requests for engineers to merge
use_cases: Auditing a repository for security, correctness and maintainability issues
Getting fixes as draft pull requests that run your tests and build first
Prioritising technical debt by severity and effort
Catching issues such as unsanitised HTML or SQL injection with cited lines

fit: lead an engineering team with a backlog of code-quality and security issues
want AI fixes delivered as reviewable pull requests rather than suggestions
already rely on CI tests that Hyrax can run before proposing a change
not_fit: want changes merged automatically: Hyrax says an engineer merges every pull request
want a self-hosted tool: Hyrax's docs say it is a hosted service with nothing to self-host
have little test coverage: its fixes lean on your own tests and build

pricing.intro: Hyrax publishes its plans in its documentation (docs.hyrax.dev/pricing), in US dollars. Both plans run on credit: each audit, fix or review draws it down by its cost.

plans.name: Free
plans.detail: No card. $30 one-time credit when the workspace is created (never expires), then $10 credit a month; unlimited members and repositories; no spending past the credit

plans.name: Paid
plans.detail: $30 of credit per seat each month (expires at the end of the period); one member per seat; optional on-demand spending, off by default and capped at $500 a period (or $15 per seat on large workspaces); missions (beta) on request

notes: Monthly credit does not roll over. The docs say the $30 signup credit is sized for one Standard audit of a typical repository.
Workspaces above 500 seats are set up by support.

alternatives.intro: CodeRabbit, Graphite and cubic are on Product Hunt's alternatives list. Review scores are Product Hunt users' own.

items.name: CodeRabbit
items.what: AI code review on pull requests
items.difference: Reviews the pull requests your team opens; Hyrax audits the whole codebase and opens its own fix pull requests.

items.name: Graphite
items.what: AI-powered pull request toolchain and review
items.difference: Built around stacked pull requests and review workflow; Hyrax focuses on finding and fixing issues.

items.name: cubic
items.difference: Review-first; Hyrax runs a full audit and remediation.

alternatives.more: Product Hunt also lists Codex 3.0 by OpenAI and Qodo.

pros: Fixes arrive as draft pull requests after your tests and build pass
Nothing merges without an engineer, per Hyrax
Audit covers six categories, scored by severity and effort
Findings cite the exact lines and go through an internal counter-check
cons: Main website blocked our requests; pricing and facts come from its public docs
Value depends on your existing test coverage and CI

x.none: We found no posts about Hyrax AI on X to link yet.

faq.a: An AI tool that learns your codebase, audits it and returns fixes as pull requests that an engineer reviews and merges.

faq.q: Does Hyrax merge code on its own?
faq.a: No, according to its Product Hunt listing: nothing auto-merges, and an engineer reviews and merges every pull request.
Hyrax's launch images say a full audit runs about 39 tools across security, correctness, maintainability, performance, architecture and operations.

Its documentation lists a free plan ($30 one-time credit, then $10 a month, no card) and a paid plan at $30 per seat a month, which comes back as $30 of monthly credit per seat. Jobs such as audits and fixes draw down the credit.
CodeRabbit, Graphite and cubic, with Codex 3.0 by OpenAI and Qodo also on Product Hunt's list.
